claim: Mellers et al. report that training, teaming and tracking were three psychological drivers of accuracy in the IARPA tournament; the abstract gives no effect sizes.
quote: Our group tested and found support for three psychological drivers of accuracy: training, teaming, and tracking.
authors: Mellers, Ungar, Baron, Ramos, Gurcay, Fincher, Scott, Moore, Atanasov, Swift, Murray, Stone, Tetlock
title: Psychological Strategies for Winning a Geopolitical Forecasting Tournament
n: two-year tournament, five research groups, thousands of forecasters
transfer: Source of the base-rate/reference-class/averaging training content; effect size not available from abstract, so each agent step must be tested on its own.

claim: Year 1 training was randomly assigned (no training, scenario training, probability training); probability training taught reference classes, bias correction and averaging of estimates.
quote: Probability training corrected cognitive biases, encouraged forecasters to use reference classes, and provided forecasters with heuristics
title: Psychological Strategies for Winning a Geopolitical Forecasting Tournament
venue: Psychological Science (as summarised in a search result)
transfer: A random-assignment design exists, so training is the best-evidenced forecasting habit; still a human result.

claim: A 2025 reanalysis with item response theory found that controlling extraneous variables substantially eliminated, reduced or even reversed the teaming and training effects on latent ability.
quote: substantially eliminated, reduced, and, in some cases, even reversed the effects of the experimental manipulations
title: Rethinking the Role of Teams and Training in Geopolitical Forecasting (reanalysis of Mellers et al. 2014)
transfer: Do not treat human training as proof that base-rate prompts help an LLM. Author order corrected from the earlier brief: Hauenstein first, Dougherty last.

claim: The same reanalysis says strategic-responding traits separate superforecasters from others, which makes the source of their edge hard to identify.
quote: latent traits associated with strategic responding can discriminate between superforecasters and non-superforecasters
title: Rethinking the Role of Teams and Training in Geopolitical Forecasting
transfer: Superforecaster habits may partly be tournament gaming; build steps on measured gains, not on the story.

claim: Satopaa, Pemantle and Ungar argue that information diversity among forecasters matters more than measurement noise, and the best extremizing amount depends on how much their information overlaps.
quote: heterogeneity stemming from people's cognitive or information diversity is often more important than measurement noise
title: Combining Probability Forecasts and Understanding Probability Extremizing through Information Diversity
transfer: Extremize an ensemble only when the attempts hold different information. Correlated samples from one model overlap heavily, so the factor should start near 1.

claim: The earlier brief cited arXiv 1501.06943; that entry was withdrawn by the authors as a revision of 1406.2148, so cite 1406.2148.
title: arXiv 1501.06943 (withdrawn)
transfer: none (citation hygiene)

claim: Wikipedia, citing Good Judgment's own site, states GJP was 35% to 72% more accurate than any other research team in IARPA-ACE; this is a promotional figure, not a peer-reviewed effect size.
quote: 35% to 72% more accurate than any other research team
title: Good Judgment Project
n: several thousand forecasters, about 100-150 questions per year
transfer: none; the headline gain came mostly from aggregation and selection, not one habit.

claim: The claim that superforecasters beat intelligence analysts by 30% comes from press reports (Ignatius, Washington Post 2013), and the Wikipedia editors note related claims are overstated in some sources.
quote: performed about 30 percent better than the average for intelligence community analysts who could read intercepts and other secret data
title: Superforecaster
transfer: none; treat as folklore, not a measured effect.

claim: Satopaa et al. 2021 (Management Science) BIN model: removing noise contributed more to forecast accuracy than reducing bias or extracting information.
title: Bias, Information, Noise (BIN) model of forecasting
transfer: Noise reduction by averaging many independent attempts is the most defensible agent step; seen only through a Wikipedia summary, read the paper before use.

claim: Mellers et al. 2015 found cognitive ability, political knowledge and open-mindedness predicted forecast accuracy, and superforecasters scored higher than other strong forecasters on intelligence and knowledge.
title: The psychology of intelligence analysis: drivers of prediction accuracy in world politics
transfer: Open-mindedness maps to a diverse-hypotheses step; seen via secondary summary only.

claim: Planning fallacy: 37 students predicted an average of 33.9 days for their thesis (27.4 best case, 48.6 worst case) but took 55.5 days on average; about 30% finished within their estimate. Reference-class forecasting is the proposed fix.
quote: actual outcomes in a reference class of similar actions
title: Planning fallacy / Reference class forecasting
venue: Wikipedia summary of Buehler et al.
transfer: Support for a base-rate anchor step on quantity and duration estimates; small sample, original not opened.

claim: Classic overconfidence studies: people claiming 100% certainty on general knowledge items were wrong about 20% of the time; nominal 90% confidence intervals often captured the answer only about 50% of the time.
authors: Lichtenstein, Fischhoff, Phillips (1982); Alpert and Raiffa (1982), via Wikipedia
title: Overconfidence effect
transfer: Baseline human overconfidence; an agent should treat its own stated confidence as uncalibrated until measured. Originals not opened.

claim: Overestimation is most likely on hard tasks and overplacement on simple tasks (hard-easy pattern).
quote: most likely to occur on hard tasks
title: Overconfidence effect
transfer: Calibration tables should be per task class and difficulty, not global (supports mechanism M6).

claim: Xiong et al. benchmarked prompting, sampling and aggregation for verbalised confidence on 5 datasets and 5 LLMs: LLMs are overconfident when verbalising, larger models calibrate better, consistency-based methods reduce overconfidence, and white-box methods win only narrowly.
quote: Empowering large language models to accurately express confidence in their answers is essential
authors: Xiong, Hu, Lu, Li, Fu, He, Hooi
title: Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty? An Empirical Evaluation of Confidence Elicitation in LLMs
transfer: Use sample-consistency to estimate confidence rather than the model's stated number.

claim: Tian et al.: for RLHF models, verbalised confidences are typically better calibrated than token conditional probabilities, often cutting expected calibration error by a relative 50%.
quote: often reducing the expected calibration error by a relative 50%
authors: Tian, Mitchell, Zhou, Sharma, Rafailov, Yao, Finn, Manning
title: Just Ask for Calibration
n: TriviaQA, SciQ, TruthfulQA; ChatGPT, GPT-4, Claude
transfer: Verbal confidence is usable on RLHF models for factual QA; it conflicts in tone with Xiong, so measure on our own tasks.

claim: Kadavath et al.: larger models are well calibrated on multiple-choice and true/false questions in the right format; self-evaluation of a proposed answer improves when the model sees several of its own samples; P(IK) struggles to calibrate on new tasks.
title: Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
transfer: Show the selector several attempts before asking it to rate one; format matters.

claim: Semantic entropy groups sampled answers by meaning and uses the entropy; it is unsupervised, uses one model, and predicts accuracy better than comparable baselines on QA.
quote: Our method is unsupervised, uses only a single model, and requires no modifications to off-the-shelf language models.
title: Semantic Uncertainty: Linguistic Invariances for Uncertainty Estimation in Natural Language Generation
transfer: Agreement of meaning-grouped probe attempts as a route/stop signal (M1).

claim: Reasoning-trained models: SFT and RL improve verbal calibration on reasoning tasks, but models give far fewer 'I don't know' answers on factual tasks and express higher confidence with shorter reasoning.
quote: models tend to express higher confidence when providing shorter or less elaborate reasoning
title: Thinking Out Loud: Do Reasoning Models Know When They're Right?
transfer: Stated confidence after a long chain is more trustworthy than after a short one; keep an abstain floor.

claim: Halawi et al.: a retrieval-augmented LM forecasting system on post-cutoff questions nears the crowd aggregate of competitive forecasters and in some settings surpasses it.
quote: nears the crowd aggregate of competitive forecasters, and in some settings surpasses it
title: Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models
n: test set of questions after model cutoffs
transfer: Retrieve, reason, then ensemble is the proven LLM forecasting pipeline.

claim: Schoenegger et al.: a crowd of 12 LLMs matched 925 human forecasters on 31 binary questions, LLM forecasts leaned well above 50% while outcomes were near even (yes-bias), and showing the human median improved GPT-4 and Claude 2 by 17-28%, though plain averaging did better.
title: Wisdom of the Silicon Crowd: LLM Ensemble Prediction Capabilities Rival Human Crowd Accuracy
transfer: Debias the yes-lean explicitly; average diverse models if more than one is allowed. Small N.

claim: ForecastBench: about 1,000 auto-generated questions with no known outcome at submission; expert forecasters outperformed the top LLM in the original paper.
quote: expert forecasters outperform the top-performing LLM
authors: Karger, Bastani, Yueh-Han, Jacobs, Halawi, Zhang, Tetlock
title: ForecastBench: A Dynamic Benchmark of AI Forecasting Capabilities
transfer: Leak-free evaluation design for any forecasting step we add.

claim: ForecastBench update: superforecasters lead the best LLM configuration by 0.017 Brier; Grok 4.20 scored 0.102 vs 0.117 for Claude 3.5 Sonnet a year earlier; projected overall parity November 2026 (95% CI January 2026 to November 2027); a crowd-adjustment step improved one ensemble by nearly 0.01 Brier.
quote: represents about one year of LLM progress
title: LLMs are closing the gap on human forecasters
transfer: Confirms the earlier brief's 0.017 figure; extrapolation is uncertain; ensemble plus crowd adjustment is the move that helps.

claim: Tetlock's Expert Political Judgment (2005) studied hundreds of experts' long-run predictions and found experts often no better than others, with foxes beating hedgehogs; I could not open a source with its numbers this session.
title: Expert Political Judgment: How Good Is It? How Can We Know?
transfer: Fox style (many models, hedge, update) supports forced divergence on open tasks; numbers need checking in the book.
